paper_context.research_question: How effective are different neural network framings (dependency parsing, sequence tagging, multi-task learning, and combined sequence/tree structures) for end-to-end computational argumentation mining, particularly compared to feature-based ILP models?
main_claims: Neural end-to-end solutions for computational argumentation mining can perform as well as or better than state-of-the-art feature-based ILP models, eliminating the need for manual feature engineering.
Framing end-to-end argumentation mining as a token-based dependency parsing problem is ineffective, yielding subpar performance.
Standard neural sequence tagging models (e.g., BiLSTMs) that encode distance information between components perform robustly across different classification scenarios for argumentation mining.
Jointly learning 'natural' subtasks in a multi-task learning setup improves performance in argumentation mining.
BiLSTM taggers are highly effective for component detection in argumentation mining.
Decoupling component and relation detection, but modeling them jointly, is more optimal than naive coupling for argumentation mining.

Relation detection is more challenging; general frameworks like LSTM-ER perform well for 'short documents' (few entities), while more constrained models are preferable for 'long documents' (many entities).
The presented work achieves new state-of-the-art results in end-to-end argumentation mining on the PE dataset from Stab and Gurevych (2016).
expected_evaluation_dimensions: Methodological soundness of neural framings and their adaptation to argumentation mining.
Empirical rigor of experimental design, evaluation metrics, and statistical significance.
Performance and effectiveness of proposed neural models compared to baselines and state-of-the-art (e.g., F1 scores for component and relation identification).
Analysis and interpretation of results, including explanations for performance differences between models and document lengths.
Novelty of applying specific neural architectures (e.g., token-based dependency parsing, distance-encoded sequence tagging) to end-to-end argumentation mining.
Reproducibility of experiments, including details on hyperparameters, software, and dataset usage.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Argument structures in the PE dataset can be approximated as trees, allowing for 'loss-less' re-linking to enforce tree structure.
supporting_evidence: argument structures often form trees, or closely resemble them

the argument structure in each essay is—almost—a tree. Since there may be several major claims, each claim connects to multiple targets, which violates the tree structure. This does not pose a problem, however, since we can “loss-lessly” re-link the claims to one of the major claims (e.g., the last major claim in a document) and create a special root node to which the major claims link.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: The dependency parsing framing, which globally enforces a tree structure, might be fundamentally mismatched to the true argumentative structure, leading to suboptimal performance or misrepresentation of relations. The 'loss-less' re-linking might introduce artifacts or oversimplifications.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Token-level processing is necessary for end-to-end AM without prior component segmentation or boundary identification.
supporting_evidence: What distinguishes our approach from these previous ones is that we operate on the token level, rather than on the level of components, because we address the end-to-end framework and, thus, do not assume that non-argumentative units have already been sorted out and/or that the boundaries of argumentative units are given.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If component-level processing with pre-segmentation were more effective or simpler, the token-level approach might introduce unnecessary complexity or noise, potentially hindering performance.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Distances between related components can be effectively encoded into sequence tagging labels, and the label set for distances will remain finite due to human cognitive limits.
supporting_evidence: The challenge in the end-to-end setting is to also include relations into the tagging scheme, which we realize by coding the distances between linked components into the tag label.

While the size of the label set Y is potentially infinite, we would expect it to be finite even in a potentially infinitely large data set, because humans also have only finite memory and are therefore expected to keep related components close in textual space.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If component distances are too varied or long-range, the label set might become too sparse or large, hindering learning. The assumption about human memory might not fully translate to model learning capacity, leading to poor generalization for less common distances.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Paragraph-level evaluation is a valid and necessary proxy for essay-level performance, especially for memory-intensive models like dependency parsers.
supporting_evidence: We train and test all parsers on the paragraph level, because training them on essay level was typically too memory-exhaustive.

Paragraphs have an average length of 66 tokens and are therefore much shorter than essays, which have an average length of 368 tokens. Thus, prediction on the paragraph level is easier than prediction on the essay level, because there are fewer components in a paragraph and hence fewer possibilities of source and target components in argument relations.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Performance on paragraphs might not accurately reflect performance on full essays, especially if long-range dependencies or global essay structure are critical. The observed 'immense' performance drop for LSTM-Parser from paragraph to essay level highlights this risk, suggesting the proxy might be insufficient for certain models.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The PE dataset of student essays is sufficiently representative for drawing general conclusions about end-to-end argumentation mining models.
supporting_evidence: We use the dataset of persuasive essays (PE) from Stab and Gurevych (2016), which contains student essays written in response to controversial topics...
Our work yields new state-of-the-art results in end-to-end AM on the PE dataset from Stab and Gurevych (2016).
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Student essays might have simpler or more constrained argumentation structures than other domains (e.g., legal texts, scientific papers, online debates), limiting the generalizability of the findings to broader AM applications.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The evaluation metric from Persing and Ng (2016) accurately reflects end-to-end AM performance, including its dependency of R-F1 on C-F1 scores.
supporting_evidence: We adopt the evaluation metric suggested in Persing and Ng (2016). This computes true positives TP, false positives FP, and false negatives FN, and from these calculates component and relation F1 scores...
We note that R-F1 scores depend on C-F1 scores because correct relations must have correct arguments.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If the metric has biases or does not capture all relevant aspects of argumentation quality (e.g., semantic correctness, coherence), the reported performance might be misleading. The inherent dependency of R-F1 on C-F1 means that errors in component detection heavily impact relation scores, potentially obscuring relation-specific model strengths or weaknesses.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript systematically investigates various neural network framings for end-to-end computational argumentation mining, comparing them against a state-of-the-art feature-based ILP model. The core argument progresses from identifying limitations of prior work (manual feature engineering, pipeline errors) to proposing neural alternatives, evaluating their performance across different architectural choices (dependency parsing, sequence tagging, multi-task learning, combined sequence/tree structures), and drawing conclusions about their relative effectiveness and suitability for different document lengths. The paper's logical flow is generally clear, moving from problem definition to proposed solutions, experimental setup, results, and discussion. Key claims regarding the superiority of neural models over ILP, the ineffectiveness of token-based dependency parsing, and the robustness of BiLSTM taggers are supported by empirical evidence. However, some explanations for observed performance differences, particularly concerning the 'local' vs. 'global' nature of models and the impact of architectural constraints, could benefit from deeper theoretical grounding or more direct empirical linkage. The reliance on paragraph-level evaluation for some models due to memory constraints also introduces a potential discontinuity in the comparison across document lengths.
logical_argument_graph: P1: Computational Argumentation Mining (AM) aims to find argumentation structures end-to-end from plain text, involving component segmentation, classification, relation identification, and relation classification.

P2: Prior state-of-the-art end-to-end AM approaches (e.g., ILP models) rely heavily on manual feature engineering and pipeline architectures, leading to issues like dataset-specific adaptation challenges and error propagation.
C1: Neural end-to-end solutions can overcome these limitations by eliminating manual feature engineering and performing as well as or better than feature-based ILP models.

M1: The paper proposes and evaluates several neural framings for end-to-end AM: token-based dependency parsing, token-based sequence tagging (STagT), multi-task learning (MTL) with STagT, and a combined sequence/tree structure model (LSTM-ER).
E1: Experiments are conducted on the PE dataset (Stab and Gurevych, 2016), evaluating models on component and relation F1 scores at both paragraph and essay levels.
R1: Token-based dependency parsing (e.g., LSTM-Parser) yields subpar performance compared to tagging models, especially on essay-level data, attributed to its global view and large search space.

R2: Standard neural sequence tagging models (BiLSTMs like STagBLCC) are robust and effective for component detection, capable of handling long-range dependencies by encoding distances into tag labels.
R3: Multi-task learning (MTL) with 'natural' subtasks (e.g., component detection) improves performance for sequence tagging models.
R4: Decoupling component and relation detection, but modeling them jointly (as in LSTM-ER), is more optimal than naive coupling.

R5: Relation detection is more challenging; general frameworks like LSTM-ER perform well on 'short documents' (paragraph level) but degrade significantly on 'long documents' (essay level) due to their generality and the increased number of possible relations. More constrained models (like STagT) are preferable for long documents.
C2: The best neural models (LSTM-ER on paragraph level, STagBLCC on essay level) achieve new state-of-the-art results on the PE dataset, outperforming the ILP baseline.
I1: Neural end-to-end AM is a viable and superior alternative to feature-based ILP, with specific architectural recommendations based on document length and task complexity.

strengths.title: Clear Problem Formulation and Motivation
strengths.description: The paper clearly articulates the limitations of previous feature-based ILP models for end-to-end argumentation mining, specifically highlighting the issues of manual feature engineering, ILP constraint design, and error propagation in pipeline architectures. This sets a strong foundation for motivating the investigation into neural alternatives.
evidence: 1 Introduction: 'Hand-crafted features pose a problem because AM is to some degree an “arbitrary” problem... Thus, feature sets would have to be manually adapted to and designed for each new sample of data, a challenging task. The same critique applies to the designing of ILP constraints. Moreover, from a machine learning perspective, pipeline approaches are problematic because they solve subtasks independently and thus lead to error propagation rather than exploiting interrelationships between variables.'

strengths.title: Systematic Exploration of Neural Framings
strengths.description: The manuscript systematically explores and compares four distinct neural framings for end-to-end AM: token-based dependency parsing, sequence tagging with distance encoding, multi-task learning, and a combined sequence/tree structure model (LSTM-ER). This comprehensive comparative analysis provides valuable insights into the suitability of different neural architectures for the task.
evidence: 1 Introduction: 'First, we frame the end-to-end AM problem as a dependency parsing problem.'
1 Introduction: 'Second, we frame the problem as a sequence tagging problem.'
1 Introduction: 'Third, we frame AM as a multi-task (tagging) problem.'
1 Introduction: 'Fourth, we evaluate the model of Miwa and Bansal (2016) that combines sequential (entity) and tree structure (relation) information...'

strengths.description: Several core claims, such as neural models outperforming ILP baselines, the ineffectiveness of token-based dependency parsing, and the robustness of BiLSTM taggers, are well-supported by quantitative results presented in Table 1 and Table 2. The F1 scores provide clear evidence for the comparative performance of the different approaches.

Table 2: MTL setups (e.g., Y-3:YC-3 F1(100%) 38.90) show improvements over single-task (Y-3 F1(100%) 34.35).

strengths.title: Insightful Analysis of Model Behavior and Limitations
strengths.description: The paper provides thoughtful hypotheses and explanations for observed performance differences, such as the LSTM-Parser's stack history, the 'local' nature of taggers, and LSTM-ER's degradation on long documents due to its generality. This analysis strengthens the understanding of why certain models succeed or fail under specific conditions.

concerns.title: Ambiguity in 'Ineffectiveness' of Dependency Parsing
concerns.description: The claim that token-based dependency parsing is 'ineffective' (C2) is primarily based on its comparative performance against sequence tagging models, rather than an absolute failure. The best parser (LSTM-Parser) is noted as 'best by far' among parsers, but its performance is then contrasted unfavorably with taggers. Furthermore, the severe performance drop on essay level is attributed to memory constraints and the complexity of a 'global view' for long sequences, which might be a practical limitation of the current implementation or dataset size rather than an inherent flaw of the dependency parsing framing itself. This weakens the logical conclusion that the framing is fundamentally 'ineffective'.
evidence: 5 Experiments (a) Dependency Parsing: 'The best parser by far is the LSTM-Parser. It is over 100% better than Kiperwasser on exact spans and still several percentage points on approximate spans.'
5 Experiments (b) Sequence Tagging: 'Overall, STagBLCC is ∼13% better than the best parser for C-F1 and ∼11% better for R-F1 on the paragraph level.'
5 Experiments (a) Dependency Parsing: 'We train and test all parsers on the paragraph level, because training them on essay level was typically too memory-exhaustive.'

5 Experiments (a) Dependency Parsing: 'Dependency parsers’ global view upon the data may be too complex a modeling in such situations and/or would require much more training data: the number of possible trees to consider on n tokens may just be too huge a search space when n is large.'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Clarify the scope of 'ineffectiveness' – whether it refers to absolute performance, comparative performance, or practical limitations. If the latter, discuss potential future work to overcome memory constraints or explore more efficient global parsing approaches. Re-evaluate the fundamental suitability of the framing versus implementation challenges.

concerns.title: Potential Bias from 'Loss-less' Tree Re-linking Assumption
concerns.description: The paper assumes that argument structures in the PE dataset are 'almost trees' and can be 'loss-lessly' re-linked to enforce a strict tree structure for dependency parsing (A1). This strong assumption, while enabling the application of dependency parsers, might fundamentally alter the true argumentative structure. If the 'loss-less' re-linking introduces artifacts or oversimplifications, it could unfairly disadvantage the dependency parsing models, potentially contributing to their observed 'subpar performance' and weakening the conclusion about their general ineffectiveness for AM.
evidence: 3 Data: 'Thus, the argument structure in each essay is—almost—a tree. Since there may be several major claims, each claim connects to multiple targets, which violates the tree structure. This does not pose a problem, however, since we can “loss-lessly” re-link the claims to one of the major claims (e.g., the last major claim in a document) and create a special root node to which the major claims link.'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide a more detailed analysis or justification for the 'loss-less' nature of the re-linking. Quantify the impact of this transformation on the original argument structures and discuss how it might affect the performance of tree-based models. Consider an ablation study or alternative representations that do not enforce strict tree structures.

concerns.title: Incomplete Justification for Tagger Superiority on Long Sequences
concerns.description: The argument that taggers 'can much better deal with the long sequences because they are largely invariant to length: every subsequence of a sequence forms a valid input to them, while the same is not true for parsers' (Section 5b) is a structural observation but lacks a direct, strong logical link to why this translates to superior performance for argumentation mining. While taggers are 'local' models, they still need to capture long-range dependencies (C3), which is a non-trivial task. The explanation for how this 'local' approach effectively captures 'long-range dependencies' through distance encoding could be more robustly elaborated to strengthen the argument's coherence.
evidence: 5 Experiments (b) Sequence Tagging: 'Our explanation is that taggers are simpler local models, and thus need less training data and are less prone to overfitting. Moreover, they can much better deal with the long sequences because they are largely invariant to length: every subsequence of a sequence forms a valid input to them, while the same is not true for parsers—a subsequence of a sequence does typically not form a tree.'

1 Introduction: 'neural sequence tagging models are in principle ideal candidates for such a framing because they can take into account long-range dependencies—something that is inherently difficult to capture with traditional feature-based tagging models such as conditional random fields (CRFs).'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Elaborate on the specific mechanisms within the BiLSTM taggers and the distance encoding scheme that enable effective capture of long-range dependencies, despite their 'local' nature. Provide a more direct logical bridge between the 'invariance to length' and superior AM performance.

concerns.title: Discontinuity in Paragraph vs. Essay Level Evaluation
concerns.description: The necessity to train and test dependency parsers only on the paragraph level due to memory constraints (A4) creates a discontinuity in the comparative evaluation. While acknowledged, this means that a direct, fair comparison of all models on the full essay level is not presented. This weakens the generalizability of conclusions drawn about the relative performance of parsers versus taggers, especially when discussing 'long documents' (essays), as the parsers' true essay-level potential (or lack thereof) is not fully demonstrated under comparable conditions.
evidence: 5 Experiments (a) Dependency Parsing: 'We train and test all parsers on the paragraph level, because training them on essay level was typically too memory-exhaustive.'

5 Experiments (a) Dependency Parsing: 'How does performance change when we switch to the essay level? For the LSTM-Parser, the best performance on essay level is 32.84%/47.44% CF1 (100%/50% level), and 9.11%/14.45% on RF1, but performance result varied drastically between different parametrizations. Thus, the performance drop between paragraph and essay level is in any case immense.'

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper investigates various neural network framings for end-to-end computational argumentation mining (AM), aiming to surpass feature-based ILP models and eliminate manual feature engineering. It explores dependency parsing, sequence tagging (with distance encoding), multi-task learning, and a combined sequence/tree model (LSTM-ER). The core reasoning posits that neural models can effectively identify argument components and relations, with sequence tagging models demonstrating robustness and multi-task learning improving performance, while token-based dependency parsing is deemed ineffective. The study evaluates these framings on the PE dataset, comparing F1 scores for component and relation identification at both paragraph and essay levels, and claims new state-of-the-art results.
logical_argument_graph: Neural end-to-end AM is a desirable goal, offering advantages over feature-based ILP models by eliminating manual feature engineering and pipeline error propagation.
Hypothesis: Different neural network framings can achieve effective end-to-end AM.
Experiment 1: Framing AM as a token-based dependency parsing problem.
Assumption (A1): Argument structures in the PE dataset can be approximated as trees, allowing for 'loss-less' re-linking to enforce tree structure.
Result (C2): This framing is ineffective, yielding subpar performance, especially on the essay level.

Reasoning: Dependency parsers, with their global view, are too complex for very long sequences (essays) and/or require significantly more training data, as evidenced by immense performance deterioration from paragraph to essay level (A4).
Experiment 2: Framing AM as a sequence tagging problem (STagT) with distance encoding.
Assumption (A3): Distances between related components can be effectively encoded into sequence tagging labels, and the label set for distances will remain finite due to human cognitive limits.
Result (C3): Standard neural sequence tagging models (BiLSTMs) perform robustly across classification scenarios, effectively capturing long-range dependencies.
Reasoning: Taggers are simpler, local models, less prone to overfitting, and more invariant to sequence length, making them suitable for long sequences.
Experiment 3: Framing AM as a multi-task learning (MTL) problem using the STagT framework.
Result (C4): Jointly learning 'natural' subtasks (e.g., component detection) improves performance.
Reasoning: Weight sharing in MTL forces the network to learn generalized representations, and de-coupling component and relation detection (but modeling jointly) is more optimal (C5).
Experiment 4: Evaluating LSTM-ER, a model combining sequential and tree structure information.
Result (C6): LSTM-ER shows excellent component detection but poor relation detection on the essay level; however, it substantially outperforms other systems on the paragraph level for both tasks.
Reasoning: LSTM-ER's generality, which considers many possible relations, becomes a disadvantage for long documents with many entities, whereas more constrained models (like STagT) are preferable.

Overall Comparison (C1): Neural end-to-end solutions (STagBLCC, LSTM-ER on paragraph level) perform as well as or better than the state-of-the-art feature-based ILP model, eliminating manual feature engineering.
Conclusion (C7): The presented work achieves new state-of-the-art results in end-to-end AM on the PE dataset.

concerns.title: Validity of 'Loss-less' Re-linking for Tree Structure
concerns.description: The assumption (A1) that argument structures, which are 'almost' trees, can be 'loss-lessly' re-linked to enforce a tree structure (e.g., connecting all claims to the last major claim, creating a special root) is a strong methodological choice. This re-linking might fundamentally alter the true argumentative structure, especially if multiple major claims are genuinely independent or if the original structure is not truly tree-like. This could introduce artifacts or oversimplifications that bias dependency parsing models towards an artificial structure, potentially contributing to their observed 'ineffectiveness' (C2) rather than reflecting a true limitation of the parsing paradigm for actual AM structures.
evidence: 3 Data: 'Thus, the argument structure in each essay is—almost—a tree. Since there may be several major claims, each claim connects to multiple targets, which violates the tree structure. This does not pose a problem, however, since we can “loss-lessly” re-link the claims to one of the major claims (e.g., the last major claim in a document) and create a special root node to which the major claims link.'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide a more detailed analysis of the impact of the re-linking strategy on the dataset's structural properties and how it might affect model learning, especially for dependency parsers. Quantify the 'loss' or distortion introduced by this transformation.

concerns.title: Limited Essay-Level Evaluation for Dependency Parsers
concerns.description: The conclusion that 'framing end-to-end argumentation mining as a token-based dependency parsing problem is ineffective' (C2) is primarily drawn from paragraph-level experiments, as training on essay level was 'typically too memory-exhaustive' (A4). While some essay-level results for LSTM-Parser are provided, the 'immense' performance drop from paragraph to essay level suggests that paragraph-level evaluation is not a reliable proxy for full essay-level performance for this model type. This limits the robustness and generalizability of the claim regarding dependency parsing's overall ineffectiveness for end-to-end AM.
evidence: 5 Experiments (a) Dependency Parsing: 'We train and test all parsers on the paragraph level, because training them on essay level was typically too memory-exhaustive.'

5 Experiments (a) Dependency Parsing: 'How does performance change when we switch to the essay level? For the LSTM-Parser, the best performance on essay level is 32.84%/47.44% CF1 (100%/50% level), and 9.11%/14.45% on RF1, but performance result varied drastically between different parametrizations. Thus, the performance drop between paragraph and essay level is in any case immense.'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Explore strategies to enable essay-level training for all dependency parsers (e.g., more efficient implementations, distributed computing, or more aggressive batching/gradient accumulation) or explicitly qualify the claim about ineffectiveness to the paragraph level or specific memory-constrained setups.

concerns.title: Heuristic Justification for Finite Distance Label Set
concerns.description: The assumption (A3) that the label set for encoding distances between components will be finite is justified by 'human finite memory.' While Figure 2 shows a distribution of distances, this is a heuristic argument, not a formal guarantee. The tail of the distribution, even if small, could still pose challenges for models if rare long-range dependencies are critical and not adequately represented or learned. The paper acknowledges 'long-range dependencies' (distances between -11 and +10) but does not explicitly detail how distances beyond a certain threshold are handled or if they are mapped to a generic 'long-distance' label, which could impact the model's ability to capture all relevant relations accurately.
evidence: 4 Models (AM as Sequence Tagging): 'While the size of the label set Y is potentially infinite, we would expect it to be finite even in a potentially infinitely large data set, because humans also have only finite memory and are therefore expected to keep related components close in textual space.'
4 Models (AM as Sequence Tagging): 'However, the figure also illustrates that there are indeed long-range dependencies: distance values between −11 and +10 are observed in the data.'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Clarify the practical limits of the distance encoding (e.g., maximum distance considered, how larger distances are handled) and discuss the potential impact of this truncation or generalization on performance for very long-range dependencies.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript presents an empirical investigation into various neural network framings for end-to-end computational argumentation mining (AM), directly comparing them against state-of-the-art feature-based ILP models. The core reasoning is that traditional AM approaches suffer from reliance on manual feature engineering and error propagation in pipeline architectures. The paper proposes and evaluates four neural framings: token-based dependency parsing, token-based sequence tagging (with distance encoding), multi-task learning (MTL) for sequence tagging, and an adaptation of the LSTM-ER model which combines sequential and tree structure information. The central findings are that neural solutions can match or exceed feature-based ILP models, token-based dependency parsing is largely ineffective for end-to-end AM, while BiLSTM-based sequence tagging (especially with distance encoding) proves robust. Furthermore, integrating 'natural' subtasks via MTL is shown to improve performance. The work incrementally advances the field by demonstrating the viability and relative effectiveness of different neural paradigms for a complex, structured prediction task, moving away from labor-intensive feature engineering.
logical_argument_graph: P1: Traditional end-to-end AM models (e.g., ILP-based) rely on manual feature engineering and suffer from pipeline error propagation.
P2: Neural networks offer an alternative, potentially eliminating manual feature engineering and enabling joint learning.
P3: Argumentation structures often resemble trees, suggesting dependency parsing as a natural framing.
P4: End-to-end AM requires token-level processing, not component-level pre-segmentation.
P5: Sequence tagging is a standard approach for entity recognition and can be extended to include relation information by encoding distances.
P6: Multi-task learning can improve performance by sharing representations and jointly learning related subtasks.
P7: The LSTM-ER model combines sequential and tree structures for entity and relation extraction, making it a suitable candidate for AM.
E1: Experiments show neural models (STagBLCC, LSTM-ER on paragraph level) achieve F1 scores equal to or higher than the ILP baseline (Table 1).
E2: Token-based dependency parsers (MST, Mate, Kiperwasser, LSTM-Parser) yield subpar performance for end-to-end AM, especially on essay level (Table 1).
E3: BiLSTM taggers (STagBLCC) perform robustly and better than parsers for C-F1 and R-F1 on paragraph level (Table 1).
E4: Multi-task learning with component and/or relation subtasks improves STagBL performance on essay level (Table 2).

E5: LSTM-ER performs exceptionally well on component detection but degrades significantly for relation detection on essay level due to its generality and the increased search space (Table 1, Figure 4).
C1: Neural end-to-end AM solutions can perform as well as or better than state-of-the-art feature-based ILP models, without manual feature engineering.
C2: Framing end-to-end AM as token-based dependency parsing is ineffective.
C3: Standard neural sequence tagging models (BiLSTMs with distance encoding) are robust and effective for AM, handling long-range dependencies.
C4: Jointly learning 'natural' subtasks in a multi-task learning setup improves AM performance.
C5: Decoupling component and relation detection, but modeling them jointly, is more optimal than naive coupling.
C6: Relation detection difficulty varies with document length; general frameworks for short documents, restrained modeling for long documents.
C7: The presented work achieves new state-of-the-art results in end-to-end argumentation mining on the PE dataset.

comparable_works.relevance: High. This work discusses frameworks for argumentation with structured arguments, specifically mentioning tree-structured arguments and dependency relations, which is highly relevant to the paper's exploration of dependency parsing and tree structures for AM.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similarity: Both works consider arguments as having structured, often tree-like, forms. Prakken's work provides a theoretical foundation for structured arguments, while the current paper empirically tests neural framings that attempt to capture such structures (e.g., dependency parsing, LSTM-ER's TreeLSTM component). Difference: Prakken's work is theoretical/logical, focusing on formalizing argumentation schemes and defeat relations. The current paper is empirical, evaluating neural models for automatic extraction of these structures from text.

comparable_works.citation_label: Aroyo, L., & Welty, C. (null). Truth Is a Lie: Crowd Truth and the Seven Myths of Human Annotation.
comparable_works.relevance: Moderate. This paper discusses ambiguity in semantic interpretation and annotator disagreement, which is indirectly relevant to the challenges of defining and annotating complex argumentation structures, as highlighted by the current paper's discussion of AM being an 'arbitrary' problem dependent on argumentation theory.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similarity: Both papers acknowledge the inherent complexity and potential for ambiguity in linguistic annotation tasks. The current paper implicitly deals with this by noting that AM datasets differ due to varying argumentation theories. Difference: Aroyo & Welty focus on the nature of disagreement in crowd-sourced annotation and its signal value. The current paper focuses on developing models to *extract* argumentation structures, assuming a given (albeit complex) annotation scheme.

uncertainty_flags: The assumption that argument structures in the PE dataset can be 'loss-lessly' re-linked to enforce a tree structure might oversimplify the true argumentative relations, potentially impacting the validity of dependency parsing results.

The expectation of a finite label set for distance encoding in sequence tagging, based on human cognitive limits, is an empirical observation rather than a theoretical guarantee, and could be challenged by more diverse or longer texts.

The reliance on paragraph-level evaluation as a proxy for essay-level performance for memory-intensive models (like dependency parsers) introduces uncertainty about their true scalability and effectiveness on full documents.

The acknowledgment that the TreeLSTM component of LSTM-ER is 'ineffective for our data' due to inter-sentence relations (92% of relations are inter-sentence) suggests a significant mismatch between the model's design and the dataset's characteristics, raising questions about the overall suitability of LSTM-ER for this specific AM task despite its strong component detection.

The paper notes that 'a model enforces a constraint does not necessarily mean that it is more suitable for a respective task' and that models 'tend to produce output consistent with constraints in their training data'. This implies that observed performance might reflect learned dataset biases rather than true structural understanding, particularly for models like dependency parsers that globally enforce tree structures.
alternative_interpretations: The subpar performance of dependency parsing might not solely be due to its 'ineffectiveness' for end-to-end AM, but rather due to the specific token-level encoding chosen, or the inherent complexity of globally enforcing a tree structure on long, complex argumentative texts with limited training data. A different dependency parsing formulation or more extensive data might yield better results.

The robustness of BiLSTM taggers could be attributed more to their local nature and ability to handle long sequences without global structural constraints, rather than their explicit encoding of distance information. The distance encoding might be a useful heuristic, but the fundamental strength could lie in the sequence modeling itself.

The improvement from multi-task learning might not be solely due to 'jointly learning natural subtasks' but also from the regularization effect of having multiple loss functions, which can prevent overfitting and encourage more generalized representations, even if the auxiliary tasks are not perfectly 'natural' or hierarchical.

The 'new state-of-the-art results' on the PE dataset should be interpreted with caution, given the specific characteristics of student essays and the potential limitations of generalizability to other argumentation domains. The incremental nature of the improvement over the ILP baseline, while significant, might not represent a paradigm shift across all AM tasks.
transparency_notes: The paper explicitly states that 'training [parsers] on essay level was typically too memory-exhaustive', leading to paragraph-level evaluation for these models. This is a practical limitation that impacts the direct comparability of parser performance with other models evaluated on essay level.

The discussion of LSTM-ER's degradation on essay-level relation detection provides a clear rationale related to the combinatorial explosion of possible relations and the model's generality, contrasting it with the more constrained STagT approach. This transparency helps understand the trade-offs.

The paper acknowledges that 'part of the TreeLSTM modeling inherent to LSTM-ER is ineffective for our data because this modeling exploits dependency tree structures on the sentence level, while relationships between components are almost never on the sentence level.' This is a crucial self-critique regarding model-data mismatch.

The paper mentions that 'another possible framing, not considered here, is to frame AM as an encoder-decoder problem' and that related research was submitted during their work. This indicates awareness of alternative, potentially more powerful, neural architectures not fully explored in this paper.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript presents an empirical investigation into various neural network framings for end-to-end computational argumentation mining (AM) at the token level, explicitly aiming to move beyond traditional feature-based Integer Linear Programming (ILP) models. The authors explore four primary neural approaches: token-based dependency parsing, sequence tagging with a novel distance-encoding scheme for relations, multi-task learning (MTL) building on sequence tagging, and a combined sequential and tree-structure model (LSTM-ER). A central tenet of the paper is the direct comparison of these neural methods against state-of-the-art ILP models, demonstrating that neural solutions can achieve comparable or superior performance while eliminating the need for manual feature engineering. Key findings include the ineffectiveness of token-based dependency parsing for end-to-end AM, the robustness and strong performance of distance-encoded BiLSTM sequence taggers (STagBLCC), and the performance benefits of incorporating 'natural' subtasks into an MTL setup for sequence tagging. The paper also discusses the varying performance of models, particularly LSTM-ER, across different document lengths (paragraph vs. essay level), attributing it to the complexity of relation detection in longer texts.
logical_argument_graph: Traditional end-to-end Argumentation Mining (AM) relies on labor-intensive manual feature engineering and Integer Linear Programming (ILP) constraints, which are prone to error propagation and lack adaptability across datasets.
Neural network approaches offer a promising alternative by automatically learning representations and facilitating joint learning, thereby addressing the limitations of feature-based ILP models.

The paper hypothesizes that different neural framings (dependency parsing, sequence tagging, multi-task learning, combined sequence/tree structures) will exhibit varying effectiveness for the end-to-end AM task at the token level.
Experiments are conducted on the PE dataset, evaluating the proposed neural framings against a state-of-the-art feature-based ILP baseline, using F1 scores for component and relation identification.

Empirical results demonstrate that: (a) token-based dependency parsing is generally ineffective for end-to-end AM, especially on longer documents; (b) standard BiLSTM sequence tagging models, particularly those encoding distance information (STagBLCC), perform robustly and can capture long-range dependencies; (c) multi-task learning with 'natural' subtasks (like component detection) significantly improves sequence tagging performance; (d) the LSTM-ER model, while strong for component detection, struggles with relation identification on longer documents due to its generality.

Overall, neural models (specifically STagBLCC and LSTM-ER on paragraph level) achieve performance comparable to or better than the feature-based ILP baseline, validating the potential of neural end-to-end AM without manual feature engineering.

The conclusion is that neural end-to-end AM is a viable and often superior approach, with sequence tagging-based methods proving more effective than token-based dependency parsing, particularly when considering document length and the benefits of task decoupling and joint modeling.

strengths.title: Conceptual Shift to End-to-End Neural AM
strengths.description: The manuscript's foundational premise, moving end-to-end argumentation mining entirely to neural, token-level processing and explicitly rejecting manual feature engineering and ILP constraints, represents a significant conceptual departure from prior pipeline-based, feature-heavy approaches. This shift challenges established practices and offers a new paradigm for the field.

strengths.title: Novel Framing of Relations via Distance Encoding in Sequence Tagging
strengths.description: The proposed method of encoding inter-component relations directly into sequence tagging labels by representing the distance ('d') and relation type ('s') alongside BIO and component type ('t') is a conceptually novel and unconventional approach for integrating complex structural information into a local token-level tagging framework. This creative solution addresses a key challenge in end-to-end AM.

strengths.title: Systematic Comparative Exploration of Neural Paradigms
strengths.description: The paper does not merely propose a single neural model but systematically explores and compares multiple distinct neural framings (dependency parsing, sequence tagging, multi-task learning, combined sequence/tree structures) for the same end-to-end, token-level AM task. This broad comparative analysis provides valuable insights into the strengths and weaknesses of different neural architectures for this complex problem.

concerns.title: Premature Dismissal of Token-Based Dependency Parsing
concerns.description: While the paper's experiments show subpar performance for token-based dependency parsers, the conclusion that this framing is 'ineffective' might be too strong. The identified limitations (memory-intensive training on essay level, large search space for long sequences, potential need for more data) suggest that the current implementations or training conditions are insufficient, rather than the framing itself being fundamentally flawed for argumentation mining. More advanced neural parsers or different training strategies might yield better results, making the dismissal potentially premature.
evidence: 5 Experiments (a) Dependency Parsing: 'We train and test all parsers on the paragraph level, because training them on essay level was typically too memory-exhaustive.'

5 Experiments (a) Dependency Parsing: 'the LSTM-Parser’s deterioration is much more severe than the other models’ surveyed below. We believe that this is due to the very long sequences encountered on essay level. Dependency parsers’ global view upon the data may be too complex a modeling in such situations and/or would require much more training data: the number of possible trees to consider on n tokens may just be too huge a search space when n is large.'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Reframe the conclusion regarding dependency parsing to acknowledge the limitations of current implementations and training conditions, rather than a definitive statement of ineffectiveness. Suggest future work exploring more robust or scalable neural dependency parsing architectures, or larger datasets, before a final judgment.

concerns.title: Scalability of Distance-Encoded Tagging for Extreme Long-Range Dependencies
concerns.description: The novel distance-encoding scheme for sequence tagging relies on the assumption that related components are typically 'close in textual space' and that the label set for distances will remain finite due to human cognitive limits. While the PE dataset supports this for observed distances, the theoretical 'potentially infinite' size of the label set for 'd' (distance) poses a novelty risk for scalability. In domains with significantly longer documents or more complex, non-local argumentative structures, this encoding might lead to an unmanageably sparse or large label space, hindering learning and generalization.
evidence: 4 Models (AM as Sequence Tagging): 'While the size of the label set Y is potentially infinite, we would expect it to be finite even in a potentially infinitely large data set, because humans also have only finite memory and are therefore expected to keep related components close in textual space.'
4 Models (AM as Sequence Tagging): 'However, the figure also illustrates that there are indeed long-range dependencies: distance values between −11 and +10 are observed in the data.'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Discuss the potential limitations and scalability challenges of the distance-encoding scheme for extremely long documents or domains with very sparse long-range dependencies. Suggest future work on adaptive distance encoding (e.g., binning or relative positions) or alternative mechanisms for handling very long-range dependencies.

concerns.title: Generalizability of Findings from PE Dataset's Tree-like Structure
concerns.description: The PE dataset's 'almost-tree' structure, and the 'loss-less re-linking' assumption (A1) to enforce a tree structure for compatibility with dependency parsing, might limit the generalizability of findings, particularly the strong dismissal of dependency parsing. If argumentation structures in other domains are less tree-like or more complex (e.g., graphs with multiple parents, cycles), the dependency parsing framing might be more fundamentally mismatched, but the current paper's preprocessing could obscure this nuance. This raises a novelty risk regarding the broader applicability of the conclusions.
evidence: 3 Data: 'Thus, the argument structure in each essay is—almost—a tree. Since there may be several major claims, each claim connects to multiple targets, which violates the tree structure. This does not pose a problem, however, since we can “loss-lessly” re-link the claims to one of the major claims (e.g., the last major claim in a document) and create a special root node to which the major claims link.'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Explicitly discuss how the specific 'almost-tree' structure of the PE dataset and the 'loss-less re-linking' might influence the generalizability of the findings, especially concerning the effectiveness of tree-based models like dependency parsers. Suggest exploring these framings on datasets with more complex, graph-like argumentation structures.

comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: This work discusses theoretical frameworks for argumentation, often involving tree structures and logical dependencies, which are conceptually related to the paper's task. However, it does not propose or evaluate computational models for end-to-end argumentation mining, especially not using neural networks at the token level. This highlights the present paper's focus on an empirical, computational approach to a problem often discussed theoretically.

Similar to Prakken (null), this work delves into formalizing argumentation, which provides a theoretical underpinning for the structures the current paper aims to extract. However, it lacks direct computational models for end-to-end argumentation mining, making the present paper's neural, empirical approach distinct in its methodology.

counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If significantly larger and more diverse argumentation datasets were available, token-based dependency parsing models might overcome their current memory and search space limitations, potentially demonstrating effectiveness for end-to-end AM.

Should future neural dependency parsers incorporate more sophisticated mechanisms for handling long-range, non-projective dependencies (e.g., advanced attention or graph neural networks), the 'ineffectiveness' finding for this framing could be reversed.

logical_argument_graph: Problem: End-to-end AM is challenging, prior work relies on manual features & ILP constraints, leading to pipeline errors.
Hypothesis: Neural models can overcome these limitations, offering end-to-end solutions without manual feature engineering.

Approach: Investigate four neural framings: token-based dependency parsing, token-based sequence tagging (with distance encoding), multi-task learning (MTL) for tagging, and LSTM-ER (combining sequence/tree).
Experiment: Evaluate these models on the PE dataset (Stab and Gurevych, 2016) using F1 scores for component and relation identification, comparing against the feature-based ILP baseline.

Finding 1 (Parsers): Token-based dependency parsing is ineffective, yielding subpar performance compared to tagging models, especially on essay level (supported by Table 1 and performance drop discussion).
Finding 2 (Taggers): BiLSTM taggers with distance encoding are robust and effective, handling long-range dependencies (supported by Table 1, Figure 4, and discussion of length invariance).
Finding 3 (MTL): Jointly learning natural subtasks (e.g., component detection) in MTL improves performance (supported by Table 2).

Finding 4 (Decoupling): Decoupling component and relation detection, but modeling them jointly (like LSTM-ER or MTL), is more optimal than naive coupling (supported by LSTM-ER's component performance and MTL improvements).

Finding 5 (Relation Difficulty): Relation detection is harder, and model suitability varies with document length (general for short, restrained for long) (supported by LSTM-ER performance drop on essay R-F1 and comparison with STagT constraints).

Conclusion: Neural end-to-end AM can match or outperform feature-based ILP (especially on paragraph level), achieving new state-of-the-art on the PE dataset, while eliminating manual feature engineering.

The heuristic justification for the finite label set in distance encoding (A3), based on 'human finite memory,' introduces theoretical uncertainty regarding its scalability and generalizability to datasets with significantly longer or more complex long-range dependencies.

Hypotheses regarding the specific reasons for observed performance differences (e.g., LSTM-Parser's stack history, taggers' local nature, LSTM-ER's degradation on long documents) are presented as plausible explanations but lack deeper empirical or theoretical validation within the paper.

The claim of 'new state-of-the-art' (C7) is specific to the PE dataset and the comparison against the ILP baseline, not necessarily implying universal state-of-the-art across all argumentation mining datasets or neural architectures.

Section: Q: Can I use generative AI?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, policy_screen
Content: The following recommendations come from the ACL policy on publication ethics. The reviewer has to read the paper fully and write the content and argument of the review by themselves, subject to the secondary reviewer policy described above, and it is not permitted to use generative assistance to create the first draft. This requirement extends to the meta-review, and the reviewer has to write any meaningful argumentation in the meta-review by themselves. Generative assistance should be used responsibly. For instance, it is reasonable to use writing assistance to paraphrase the review, e.g. to help reviewers who are not native speakers of English. It is also reasonable to use tools that help to check proofs. Neither reviewers nor editors should upload a submitted manuscript or any part of it into a non-privacy preserving generative tool as this may violate the authors’ confidentiality and intellectual property rights and, where the paper contains personally identifiable information, may breach data privacy rights. This confidentiality requirement extends to the peer review report, as it may contain confidential information about the manuscript and/or the authors. For this reason, neither reviewers nor editors may upload their peer review report into a non-privacy-preserving generative tool, even if it is just for the purpose of improving language and readability. The ACL publication ethics committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct.

Section: Q: Can I use generative AI?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, policy_screen
Content: The following recommendations come from the ACL policy on publication ethics. The reviewer has to read the paper fully and write the content and argument of the review by themselves, subject to the secondary reviewer policy described above, and it is not permitted to use generative assistance to create the first draft. This requirement extends to the meta-review, and the reviewer has to write any meaningful argumentation in the meta-review by themselves. Generative assistance should be used responsibly. For instance, it is reasonable to use writing assistance to paraphrase the review, e.g. to help reviewers who are not native speakers of English. It is also reasonable to use tools that help to check proofs. Neither reviewers nor editors should upload a submitted manuscript or any part of it into a non-privacy preserving generative tool as this may violate the authors’ confidentiality and intellectual property rights and, where the paper contains personally identifiable information, may breach data privacy rights. This confidentiality requirement extends to the peer review report, as it may contain confidential information about the manuscript and/or the authors. For this reason, neither reviewers nor editors may upload their peer review report into a non-privacy-preserving generative tool, even if it is just for the purpose of improving language and readability. The ACL publication ethics committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct.

Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: Q: Can I use generative AI?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, policy_screen
Content: The following recommendations come from the ACL policy on publication ethics. The reviewer has to read the paper fully and write the content and argument of the review by themselves, subject to the secondary reviewer policy described above, and it is not permitted to use generative assistance to create the first draft. This requirement extends to the meta-review, and the reviewer has to write any meaningful argumentation in the meta-review by themselves. Generative assistance should be used responsibly. For instance, it is reasonable to use writing assistance to paraphrase the review, e.g. to help reviewers who are not native speakers of English. It is also reasonable to use tools that help to check proofs. Neither reviewers nor editors should upload a submitted manuscript or any part of it into a non-privacy preserving generative tool as this may violate the authors’ confidentiality and intellectual property rights and, where the paper contains personally identifiable information, may breach data privacy rights. This confidentiality requirement extends to the peer review report, as it may contain confidential information about the manuscript and/or the authors. For this reason, neither reviewers nor editors may upload their peer review report into a non-privacy-preserving generative tool, even if it is just for the purpose of improving language and readability. The ACL publication ethics committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct.
